prayer.text: Saint Teresa of Ávila, pray for us.

cues.text: A Reluctant Vocation
Born in 1515 to a merchant family of partly Jewish converso ancestry in Ávila , Teresa entered the Carmelite Convent of the Incarnation at twenty.

She did so not from any burning attraction to religious life but, as she later admitted with characteristic honesty, from a desire to choose the safest path to salvation rather than risk an uncertain life in the world.

For nearly two decades her spiritual life remained lukewarm, divided between the convent's comfortable, socially permissive routine — the Incarnation allowed private apartments, visitors, and considerable personal property — and genuine but inconsistent efforts at deeper prayer.
Conversion and Mystical Experience
Around 1554, in her late thirties, Teresa underwent a profound interior conversion before an image of the wounded Christ.
Afterward, her prayer life deepened dramatically into states of mystical union she would later describe with unusual psychological precision in her writings.
She experienced visions, locutions, and the famous transverberation — a mystical wounding of the heart by a seraphic angel, an event later immortalized in Bernini's sculpture in Rome.

Wary of self-deception and aware of the Spanish Inquisition's suspicion of visionary women, Teresa submitted her experiences repeatedly to confessors and theologians for scrutiny, a caution that helped protect both her reputation and her later writings from formal censure.
Reforming Carmel
Disturbed by the laxity she saw around her, Teresa resolved to found a new convent observing the primitive Carmelite rule in its original austerity.

Despite fierce opposition from ecclesiastical and civic authorities in Ávila, who saw an unauthorized new foundation as a threat to public order, she opened the convent of St. Joseph in 1562 with four nuns living in strict poverty and enclosure.
Over the following two decades, Teresa founded seventeen convents of what became known as the Discalced ("shoeless") Carmelites .
Often traveling by mule cart across Spain in poor health, she recruited the young friar John of the Cross in 1568 to extend the reform to the male branch of the order.
A Writer of Genius
Ordered by her confessors to write an account of her life and prayer, Teresa produced some of the most original works of Spanish mystical literature.
She wrote them largely in the margins of an exhausting administrative career: The Book of Her Life , The Way of Perfection , and, above all, The Interior Castle .
The latter is an extended allegory of the soul's journey toward God through seven concentric "mansions" of prayer.

Written in vivid, plainspoken Castilian rather than academic Latin, her works combined precise psychological observation with genuine theological depth, and remain among the most widely read texts in the entire Catholic mystical tradition.
Legacy
Teresa died at Alba de Tormes on October 4, 1582, the night the Gregorian calendar reform took effect, so that the following day was reckoned October 15 — the date that became her feast.
She was canonized in 1622.
In 1970, Pope Paul VI declared Teresa the first woman ever named a Doctor of the Church .
This formally recognized what generations of readers had long known: this once-reluctant nun from Ávila had become one of the surest guides to prayer the Catholic tradition possesses.
